column3: It directly contrasts the true call with calls that receive no response, clarifying the focus's denial of any valid rival call.
Entry into the Garden supplies only a broad opposite final abode to the Fire-companionship named in the focus.
Its confession of excess and plea for forgiveness gives a repentant counterpart to the focus's excessive ones.
The immediately preceding speech rejects the call to association and answers it with a call to God, directly framing the focus.
The accusation against the messenger opens Pharaoh's narrative but adds nothing specific to the focus's call, return, or Fire outcome.
Gathering God's enemies toward the Fire supplies a direct judgment-scene horizon for the focus's Fire companions.
Its formulaic declaration of loss in the Hereafter supports the consequence horizon but adds little beyond it.
An answered invocation and the command to remain straight provide a faithful contrast to the invalid call rejected in the focus.
It names excessive conduct after speaking of killing and preserving life, but does not develop the focus's final destination.
The declaration of utmost Hereafter loss is a general parallel to the focus's final consequence.
The same surah's account of proportionate recompense and Garden entry clarifies the moral alternatives behind the focus's Fire outcome.
The Fire is depicted as calling those who turn away, an adverse counterpart to the competing calls in the focus.
Preferring worldly life and rejecting guidance explains a route toward the loss in the Hereafter implied by the focus.
Garden entry for believers is a broad contrast to the focus's Fire-companion destination.
A caller summons people to an overwhelming event, giving an eschatological counterpart to the focus's language of calling.
It states that some have nothing in the Hereafter but Fire, directly reinforcing the focus's final consequence.
It identifies disbelief when God alone was called as the cause of judgment, directly completing the rival-call conflict in the focus.
The messenger's call to faith shows the responsive alternative to the rejected call in the focus.
God's rejection of the arrogant supplies only a general moral backdrop for the Fire consequence.
False counsel ends in abiding in the Fire, providing a consequence pattern for the focus's Fire companions.
It warns that following others can return believers to disbelief, but its social setting is indirect.
The prohibition on obeying the excessive directly characterizes the group the focus assigns to the Fire.
Those called to faith but disbelieving are condemned in the same surah, directly grounding the focus's opposing-call consequence.
Following disbelievers back into unbelief is a distant counterpart to the wrong invitation rejected in the focus.
The shared decisive formula and assignment to the Fire support the focus's final declaration, though less specifically.
Its prayer recognizes that entry into the Fire brings disgrace and leaves wrongdoers without helpers, closely framing the focus's Fire fate.
Fire here is a created substance rather than the final abode at issue in the focus.
It rejects calling what cannot benefit or harm and redirects toward God's guidance, directly paralleling the focus's invalid rival call.
The provision of livestock in the same surah does not add to the focus's call, return, or Fire consequence.
The arrival of an irreversible punishment gives a limited judgment backdrop to the focus's final declaration.
Pharaoh is identified as one of the excessive, a concrete instance of the category named in the focus.
It explicitly contrasts Fire companions with Garden companions, directly clarifying the final identity asserted in the focus.
Questioning a return to a former state offers only an indirect resurrection-related parallel.
It identifies persistent offenders as abiding Fire companions, reinforcing the consequence category in the focus.
The immediately preceding contrast between a call to salvation and a call to Fire directly sets up the focus's verdict on the latter.
It announces Fire punishment for disbelievers but adds little after the stronger Fire-destination cards.
Calling God in distress, then reverting to rivals and becoming a Fire companion, traces a meaningful reversal behind the focus's warning.
Forgiveness and honor for a witness provide only a broad positive contrast to the focus's negative destination.
The allegedly called beings vanish when needed, directly illustrating the focus's claim that they possess no valid call.
Deliverance of some and destruction of the excessive supplies a consequence parallel for the category named in the focus.
The same surah's contrast between believers and evildoers gives a moral frame for the final division in the focus.
Its command not to exceed limits directly supplies a conduct-level contrast to the focus's excessive ones.
It rejects worship of powerless objects, commands worship of God, and states return to Him, closely matching all three focus movements.
The isolated mention of right-side companions does not clarify the rival call or return in the focus.
It asks whether anyone can rescue one already in the Fire, directly delimiting the consequence named in the focus.
Pharaoh is again called excessive while a vulnerable group believes, offering a contextual example but no final-fire scene.
The greatness of creation provides nearby support for divine power but does not address the focus's rival call.
Death culminates in return to the knower of all, directly clarifying the focus's declaration that all return to God.
Its world-versus-Hereafter contrast and severe punishment give a broad value horizon for the focus's final consequence.
Neither wealth nor children can avail against God, and the offenders are abiding Fire companions, directly reinforcing the focus's outcome.
The warning to guard against a Fire fueled by people gives a preventative counterpart to the focus's Fire assignment.
Apostasy ending in abiding Fire companionship supplies a clear consequence parallel, though it repeats the established pattern.
The condemned confess their condition and seek a way out, providing the same-surah final voice from which the focus's Fire verdict is understood.
Ordinary creation, death, and senility do not materially clarify return or the validity of calls.
It rejects association, directs one toward repentance, and affirms return to God, a coherent alternative to the focus's rejected call.
The brief category of right-side companions does not add a specific relation to the focus.
Creation's purpose and the woe from Fire provide only a general theological backdrop.
All intercession belongs to God and all return to Him, reinforcing the focus's return while limiting rival reliance.
The greeting to right-side companions adds no focused relation after the earlier destination contrasts.
Being dragged into the Fire vividly specifies punishment but is redundant with stronger Fire-destination evidence.
The movement from light to darkness and final Fire companionship contrasts God's guidance with the false direction rejected in the focus.
The faithful ask protection from Fire, offering a devotional counterpart to the focus's final Fire judgment.
The attack of fire and molten metal is a punishment image without a focused call or return relation.
God answers the caller and commands response to Him, directly contrasting the focus's declaration that rival calls have no standing.
The same surah affirms that all return to God after divine promises are fulfilled, directly supporting one focus clause.
It explicitly calls transgressors excessive, giving a concrete behavioral instance of the category in the focus.
Recompense for what hands have sent forward provides an accountability rationale for the focus's Fire consequence.
Sins lead to entry into Fire with no helpers besides God, a close consequence parallel to the focus's Fire companions.
The beings called besides God possess nothing, directly supporting the focus's denial of their claim or response.
A people reject and doubt what their messengers call them toward, supplying a call-and-rejection pattern behind the focus.
God judges by truth while those called besides Him decide nothing, directly restating the focus's invalid-rival-call logic.
The same surah explicitly identifies disbelievers as Fire companions, directly reinforcing the focus's final clause.
No protector, intercessor, or ransom can avert earned punishment, supplying a constraint on the focus's final outcome.
The call to a companion in an animal-story episode does not clarify the focus's theological call.
Noah's public call to his people is too general to add to the focus's rival-call and final-judgment scene.
It denies purposeless creation and affirms return to God, directly supporting the focus's return clause.
The same surah's decisive divine judgment gives only broad nearby context for the focus.
Disbelievers abiding in Hell repeat the Fire-companion consequence with little additional specification.
Inheritance rules and numerical shares do not clarify the focus.
The state of those in the Fire adds a punishment detail but is redundant with earlier direct destination texts.
The prepared Fire for disbelievers reinforces the destination in the focus, though without its call logic.
Personal striving and recompense offer a broad accountability premise but no focused link to the Fire companions.
The same surah presents continual exposure to Fire and final entry into severe punishment, strongly situating the focus's outcome.
It challenges whether the invoked objects can hear their callers, directly probing the invalid call asserted in the focus.
God's call brings people forth from the earth, supplying a decisive divine-call contrast and a resurrection horizon for return.
Hearing the caller, believing, and seeking forgiveness supplies a faithful response pattern opposite the focus's rejected call.
The rebuke to Fire-deniers confirms judgment recognition but adds little to the focus's logic.
The warning that sins may bring affliction provides only a broad accountability connection.
Disbelievers are abiding Fire companions, a direct but repeated restatement of the focus's consequence.
A prophet's repeated call to his people does not materially clarify the focus's rival call or final return.
Fire companions appeal to Garden companions and are refused, closely portraying a futile plea from within the final state.
The prohibition on calling another god, with punishment as consequence, directly supports the focus's rejection of rival invocation.
Past destruction and the better Hereafter for the mindful provide only a general consequence backdrop.
Guidance's increase and the better final return offer a distant positive contrast to the focus's failed destination.
The guilty see the Fire and find no diversion away from it, directly constraining the final fate named in the focus.
The description of intensely hot fire adds no meaningful relation beyond the already established destination.
Quranic guidance and reward offer a broad positive alternative but do not specify the focus's call or Fire logic.
Every community is called to its record for recompense, furnishing an accountability scene related to the focus's final verdict.
Pre-Islamic zeal and the believers' tranquility do not add to the focus's call, return, or Fire consequence.
Fire as a claimed material of superiority in Iblis's reply does not clarify the focus's final Fire companionship.
God commands direct invocation and promises response, while the arrogant enter Hell; this is the clearest omitted counterpart to the focus's invalid rival call and Fire outcome.
It calls those who invoke beings that cannot answer until the Resurrection the most astray, directly elaborating the focus's denial of a rival call in both worlds.
The invoked beings become enemies and reject their worshippers when humanity is gathered, directly extending the focus's final failure of rival invocation.
Those called besides God neither hear nor answer, and will deny the association on the Day of Resurrection, closely matching the focus's world-and-Hereafter claim.
Those called besides God are servants unable to answer their callers; it directly tests the legitimacy of the invocation rejected in the focus.
It forbids calling what neither benefits nor harms apart from God, directly supplying the practical prohibition behind the focus's verdict.
Whoever calls another god without proof faces reckoning with God, directly joining forbidden invocation to the focus's return clause.
It prohibits calling anyone alongside God, directly stating the exclusive-invocation rule assumed by the focus.
On the Day God asks where the alleged partners are, the verse supplies a direct final-judgment challenge to the rival call rejected in the focus.
The repeated question about alleged partners at the gathering reinforces the final exposure of those called besides God.
In distress at sea people lose sight of those they call besides God, directly illustrating the unreliability of rival invocation.
The beings invoked besides God create nothing and are themselves created, directly grounding the focus's denial of their valid claim.
Calling what cannot harm or benefit is named manifest error, a direct parallel to the focus's rival-call judgment.
God alone is the True, while what is called besides Him is false, directly articulating the contrast behind the focus.
The alleged partners possess no atom's weight in the heavens or earth, directly supporting the focus's denial of their standing.
God gives life and death and brings a decree into being, adding a close same-surah account of divine sovereignty before the universal return named in the focus.
Those who were arrogant enter the gates of Hell to abide there, a direct same-surah completion of the Fire-companion consequence.
Those who deny the Book and what was sent with messengers are directed toward the later punishment sequence, supplying the immediate same-surah cause of the Fire fate.
God gives life and death and declares that the final return is to Him, directly restating the focus's return clause.
God answers the distressed caller and removes harm, furnishing a positive counterpart to the focus's claim that false addressees possess no call.
God answers those who believe and act rightly, supporting the responsive divine call that contrasts with the focus's invalid alternatives.
Those who reject divine signs and act arrogantly are Fire companions abiding there, directly reinforcing the focus's consequence for transgression.
The arrogant rejecters cannot enter the Garden and are recompensed as criminals, adding a detailed counterpart to the Fire destination.
The wealth and children of disbelievers cannot avail them before God, and they are Fire companions abiding there, reinforcing the final consequence.
